title_original: Rooted in Memory: Anina Major and the Living Language of Weaving

blocks.text: At Pérez Art Museum Miami, Anina Major’s ‘The Sacred Mangrove’ explores Bahamian cultural heritage, ancestral knowledge and the relationship between material traditions and contemporary sculpture.

What happens when the knowledge carried through generations is transformed into something new? In ‘The Sacred Mangrove ‘ , Bahamian artist Anina Major reimagines traditional palm weaving through monumental ceramic sculptures, creating an immersive landscape that considers memory, migration and cultural continuity. Drawing on the plaiting practices passed down by her grandmother, Major challenges the distinctions between craft and fine art while questioning how cultural value is assigned and preserved. Through woven clay structures, bottle trees and references to Caribbean ecologies, the exhibition examines the relationships between ancestry, labour, spirituality and belonging.

In conversation with ART AFRICA , Major reflects on the enduring intelligence of traditional practices, the complexities of representing Bahamian identity, and how cultural knowledge continues to evolve across generations and geographies. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.caption: Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.text: Brendon Bell-Roberts: At the centre of ‘The Sacred Mangrove’ is your transformation of weaving from an organic, flexible practice into one shaped through fired clay. What becomes possible when you translate a material tradition associated with impermanence into something enduring?

Anina Major: I find the relationship between permanence and impermanence fascinating because neither material is entirely one or the other. Palm is organic and eventually biodegrades, while clay begins soft and vulnerable before undergoing an extraordinary transformation through fire. It becomes permanent, yet remains fragile. Initially, working with clay was a way of maintaining a connection to my grandmother after her passing. I was watching the few straw objects she left behind slowly deteriorate, and I became curious about what might happen if I translated those gestures into another material. What emerged was more than a way of preserving a form. Clay introduced its own possibilities for scale, structure, and expression. It allowed me to reconsider how we encounter these familiar objects and the value we assign to the knowledge embedded within them. With ‘The Sacred Mangrove’, that exploration has expanded beyond individual sculptures into an entire landscape. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.caption: Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.text: Weaving carries histories of labour, knowledge and ancestry within Bahamian culture. How do you approach these histories in your practice, especially when working with traditions that continue to evolve across generations?

I grew up understanding plaiting through the women around me, particularly my grandmother. It was part of her everyday life, a skill that required patience, ingenuity, and an incredible understanding of material. As I began researching the practice more deeply, I became interested in how much knowledge was being communicated through the hands. Plaiting is mathematical, structural, economic, and cultural all at once. There are histories embedded in the patterns, but there is also tremendous individuality in how those patterns are interpreted. Every generation makes its own contributions, whether through changes in material, technique, or purpose. My work is another contribution to that ongoing conversation. Anina Major, ‘ Water Tower ‘, 2024. Glazed stoneware, melted sea glass and sand. Collection Pérez Art Museum Miami, museum purchase with funds provided by PAMM’s Collectors Council. blocks.text: The exhibition considers the relationship between cultural traditions and the Bahamas’ representation within the tourism economy. How has this tension shaped how you think about value, visibility and cultural identity in your work?

Growing up in The Bahamas, tourism was an unavoidable part of how we understood ourselves and how the rest of the world encountered us. The image of paradise is incredibly powerful, but it can also flatten the complexity of a place and the people who inhabit it. A plaited object sold in the Straw Market as a souvenir had the ability to embody extraordinary history and skill. Within another context, the conversation around its value shifts. It’s this discourse that inspired this body of work. Questioning the systems that determine what we celebrate, what we overlook, and whose contributions are recognised. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.caption: Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.text: Mangroves occupy an important space within Caribbean ecologies, existing between land and water while providing protection, shelter and interconnected systems of life. What drew you to the mangrove as a framework for this exhibition, and what meanings does it hold in the work?

For ‘The Sacred Mangrove’, I was thinking about the landscape as both a physical environment and a metaphor for those interconnected systems of support, protection, and transformation. Mangroves are environments that resist simple definitions. They exist between land and water, constantly negotiating changing conditions, yet they support incredibly complex systems of life. The roots intertwine, creating structures that offer protection and stability while allowing other forms of life to flourish. Could this offer another way of considering how cultural traditions endure? They don’t necessarily survive by remaining unchanged, but through adaptation, exchange, and the relationships that sustain them. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.caption: Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.text: The installation brings together towering woven clay forms, bottle trees, crushed conch shells and Water Tower . How do these objects and materials speak to one another within the exhibition space?

I see the exhibition as a landscape rather than a collection of individual sculptures. Each element contributes to the environment, and their relationships become just as important as the objects themselves. The woven ceramic structures establish a sense of monumentality, while the bottle trees introduce associations with protection and spiritual practices within the African diaspora. The crushed conch shells and ceramic shards contribute metaphorical meaning that grounds the work beyond a surface upon which the sculptures are displayed. Water Tower draws from a historic landmark in Nassau associated with water and sustenance. Within the exhibition, it takes on another relationship to the surrounding forms. I’m interested in how these different elements begin to create a sense of place without necessarily representing a specific location. Together, they suggest an environment shaped by histories of labour, survival, spirituality, and our relationships with the natural world. Anina Major, ‘ Water Tower ‘, 2024. blocks.text: Your practice moves between categories often described separately as craft, sculpture and installation. How do you understand these distinctions in your own work, and what happens when they overlap?

Rarely, do I think about whether my work belongs to craft, sculpture, or installation while I’m making it. Those distinctions can feel quite restrictive to the creative process. Plaiting carries extraordinary intelligence, yet practices associated with women, domestic labour, or communities outside dominant art histories have often been categorised differently. I’m curious what happens when those hierarchies are challenged, particularly through material and scale. Some of the objects and artworks I admire most blur these distinctions, and history has shown that objects can move between categories depending on who is looking, where they’re presented, and when. My practice has evolved from individual ceramic sculptures toward environments that engage with landscape. I don’t see that as leaving craft behind. Rather, I want to see how far the structural language of plaiting can extend and what new possibilities emerge along the way. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.caption: Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.text: Ideas of memory and belonging recur throughout your practice. How has living and working between the Bahamas and New York shaped how you think about place, distance and the preservation or transformation of cultural knowledge?

Leaving The Bahamas made me much more conscious of the ways place shapes our understanding of ourselves. There are things you take for granted when you’re surrounded by them, and distance has a way of bringing those things into focus. But living away also complicates your relationship with home. You change, the place you left changes, and eventually you recognise that returning doesn’t necessarily mean recovering something exactly as you remember it. That experience has influenced how I think about cultural traditions. It may be impossible to preserve something exactly as it was, but how it continues to evolve as people move between places and encounter different influences- well, that’s intriguing. Portrait of Anina Majors. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.caption: Portrait  of Anina Majors. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

blocks.text: As visitors move physically through ‘ The Sacred Mangrove ‘ , what role does their encounter with the installation’s scale, materiality and spatial arrangement play in how the work unfolds?

Working at a larger scale has fundamentally changed my relationship to the work. With smaller objects, the encounter can be quite intimate. You stand outside the work and observe it. But an environment asks something different of you. You have to physically negotiate the space, moving around and between. In ‘The Sacred Mangrove’, the arrangement of the sculptures, the ground beneath them, and the spaces between them are all part of the experience. The viewer’s body becomes a measure of the work, and their movement changes with what they notice.
This exhibition is on view at the Pérez Art Museum Miami , in Florida, until 1 August 2027.
